BE PREPARED
Passengers should follow all commands and signals
given by crewmembers. Be ready to assist crewmem-
bers in an emergency and to follow the guidelines
below:
1) Know where all the exits are on this aircraft. Study the
briefing card and know how to open the exit closest
to you. Ask a crewmember if you have any questions
about this
2) Remember, keep your head down until the aircraft
has come to a complete stop. Don't be tempted to
look up and around until you are certain that the air-
craft is no longer moving.
3) If an emergency evacuation is necessary, and if a
crewmember cannot get to the exit in your row, you
have have to open it. First look outside. If fire,
the exit, don't open it. Choose another exit.
4) If it is safe to open the exit, do so as quickly as possi-
ble. Keep the pathway to the exit clear. If the exit can-
not be opened, go to another exit.
5) When the exit is open, shout "Unfasten seatbelts!
Come this way!" then go out the exit as quickly as
possible.
6) Don't take any carry-on baggage with you. It only
gets in the way and impedes the evacuation.
7) If there is not immediate danger, help the people
behind you out. Direct the passengers away from any
dangers, such as fire, smoke, or water.
8) Move 300 yards away from the aircraft as soon and
as quickly as you can.

TO SIT IN A EXIT ROW
In order to ensure the fastest possible emergency
evacuation, the Federal Aviation Administration has set
standards for people who sit in rows next to exits. In the
event of an emergency, these passengers may be called
upon to assist crewmembers in the evacuation.
Passengers sitting in exit row seats must be willing
and able to do the following:
1) Locate the emergency exit and move quickly to it;
2) Recognize the opening mechanism, comprehend
the instructions, then open the exit at the proper time;
3) Decide if opening the exit will increase hazards to
passengers;
4) Follow instructions given by crewmembers;
5) Stow the exit doors;
6) Pass quickly through the door and then
assess,
select and follow a safe path away from the aircraft.
In order to perform all of these functions, passengers
sitting in emergency exit rows must:
1) Read English well enough to understand the instruc-
tions for opening exits and for other emergency pro-
cedures
2) See well enough to read instructions, to see signals
emergency;
5) Be able to use both hands, both arms and both legs.
as well as be strong and flexible enough to do the fol-
lowing:
a. Be able to quickly open the exit. This will require
that you be able to reach up, sideways and down
and be able to grasp the door mechanism;
b. Be able to lift the exit door out of the exit; some
window hatches that must be lifted can weigh as
much as 65 pounds (30 Kgs.), the average
weight of a 7 year old child;
c. Be able to clear from the exit any obstructions
weighing up to 65 pounds and to maintain bal-
ance while doing so;
d. Be able to quickly move to and through the exit;
e. Be able to help other passengers away from the
plane;
6) Be at least 15 years of age;
7) Have the capacity to perform these functions without a
companion or adult;
8) Be with no one that requires your care, such as a small
child, or someone physically or mentally unable to

9) You must be willing and able to do all of these things
by yourself and without harming yourself.
If you cannot or do not wish to do all these things,
you cannot sit in an emergency exit row seat. If you
are already seated there, ask a crewmember to move
you to another seat. You do not have to explain why. You
need to say only "I do not want to sit in an exit row."
PORTABLE ELECTRONIC DEVICES
Atlantic
Southeast Airlines
and the Federal
Aviation
Administration restrict the use of certain portable electronic
devices on board the aircraft, as they can interfere with the nav-
igation and communication systems on the aircraft. Please be
certain that all devices are in the "OFF" position during taxi, take
off and landing.
The following devices are permitted only at cruise altitude when
the Captain has turned off the seatbelt sign. They should be
turned off at all other times:
Personal computers and computer games
VHF scanner receivers
Tape players that do not have AM/M capability
Video recorders
Calculators
CD players
The following devices may not be used at any time on the air-
craft:
Cellular telephones
Two-way radios (CB, Ham, or Walkie Talkie)
49 MHz transmitters
Remote controlled toys
External computer devices, such as mouse, joy stick, or
printer
AM/FM radios or TV's
Any other device which the crew suspects may interfere with
the aircraft systems
Passengers must comply with all crewmember instructions
Atlantic Southeast Airlines appreciates your cooperation.
